translation: There is NO natural number C with the following property: for all sufficiently large natural n (eventually along atTop), there exists a 3-uniform hypergraph H on the vertex set Fin n = {0,...,n-1} such that n - C <= ncard(cliqueSizes H). Here n - C is truncated natural-number subtraction (equal to 0 when C >= n), and ncard is the cardinality of the set of clique sizes of H (the set of natural numbers that occur as sizes of cliques of H, per the definition UniformHypergraph.cliqueSizes); ncard would be 0 if that set were infinite (it is finite here since the vertex set is finite).

(Asserted as true, not negated.) For every set A of natural numbers such that 0 is not in A and the upper density of A is strictly positive, there exists a finite set S of natural numbers with S a subset of A such that the sum over n in S of 1/n equals 1, where each n is cast to the rationals and 1/n is exact rational division (not truncated).

There is NO real number C such that: for every natural d, every type V with a Fintype instance and every simple graph G on V, if the maximum degree of G is <= d then sizeRamsey(G, G) (cast to a real) <= C * |V| (the number of vertices, cast to a real). Quantifier order: C is chosen before d, so a single C must work for all d; since d is arbitrary the degree hypothesis imposes no real restriction, i.e. the statement says there is no constant C with sizeRamsey(G,G) <= C*|V| for all finite graphs G.

For every type V (any universe, not necessarily finite), every simple graph G on V and every natural k: if ncard(set of odd cycle lengths of G) <= k, then (i) the chromatic number of G (in extended naturals, possibly infinity) is <= 2k+2, and (ii) the chromatic number equals 2k+2 if and only if the complete graph on Fin(2k+2) is contained in G (as a subgraph copy, IsContained). Junk value caveat: ncard of an infinite set is 0, so if G has infinitely many distinct odd cycle lengths the hypothesis holds for every k, including k = 0.

There exists a strictly increasing function a : N -> N such that (1) the range of a is a minimal set (with respect to inclusion: no proper subset has the property) among sets of naturals satisfying IsAsymptoticAddBasisOfOrder 2 (asymptotic additive basis of order 2), and (2) there is a real c != 0 such that the sequence n |-> ((a n / n^2 : N) cast to R) tends to c as n -> infinity. Important: a n / n^2 is computed in the natural numbers with truncating (floor) division before being cast to R (and at n = 0 it is a 0 / 0 = 0). Since the sequence takes integer values, convergence to c != 0 means floor(a n / n^2) is eventually equal to a fixed positive integer c.

It is NOT the case that: for every type V with Fintype instance and every simple graph G on V, if G is K5-free (CliqueFree 5: no clique of size 5) and 4 <= cochromatic number of G, then chromatic number of G <= cochromatic number of G + 2. Equivalently, there exists a finite graph G that has no 5-clique, has cochromatic number >= 4, and has chromatic number > cochromatic number + 2 (comparisons in the extended naturals / the types of these invariants).

There exists c > 0 (a real, since it multiplies a real) such that for every natural n and every simple graph G on the vertex set Fin(2^n) (with decidable adjacency): if every vertex v has degree (cast to R) strictly greater than (1 - c) * 2^n (real arithmetic), then the n-dimensional hypercube graph Q_n is contained in G (IsContained: G has a subgraph isomorphic to Q_n). Note c is fixed before n.

For every natural p that is prime and p != 2, there exists a natural q such that q is prime, q < p, and the multiplicative order of q (cast into ZMod p) equals p - 1 (natural subtraction; no truncation since p >= 3). I.e. every odd prime p has a prime primitive root smaller than p.

There exists a real c > 0 such that for every natural r >= 2, every natural n and every family H of finite subsets of Fin n: if H is r-uniform (every edge has exactly r elements) and H has hypergraph chromatic number 3 (HasHypergraphChromaticNumber 3, per its definition), then there is a vertex v in Fin n whose degree in H (number of edges containing v, cast to R) is >= 1 + c^r. Note the bound is 1 + c^r (c raised to r, plus 1), not (1+c)^r. Since c is fixed first, it must work for all r. (If n = 0 no vertex exists, so the conclusion requires the hypothesis to fail there.)

For every natural k >= 3, there exists a finite set A of points of R^2 (modelled as Fin 2 -> R) such that for every 2-coloring C : A -> Fin 2 there exists a finite set S of points with S a subset of A, S collinear, |S| >= k, the condition (for all y in A, y in S -> y in affineSpan(S)) which is trivially true since every point of S lies in its own affine span (so it does NOT require S to contain all points of A on the line), and a color c such that every x in S has C(x) = c. Effectively: some k collinear points of A are monochromatic.

It is NOT the case that for every function f : R -> Fin 2 (2-coloring of the reals) there exists an infinite set A of reals such that for all a, b, c, d in A with a != b and c != d, f(a+b) = f(c+d). Equivalently: there is a 2-coloring of R such that no infinite set A has all sums of two distinct elements of the same color.

For every finite set A of points in the plane R^2 (Euclidean plane) that is convex independent (ConvexIndep: no point of A lies in the convex hull of the other points, per the definition), |A| / 2 <= distinctDistances A, where |A| is cast to R and divided by 2 in the reals (no truncation), and distinctDistances A is the number of distinct distances determined by pairs of points of A (as defined; whether distance 0 is counted depends on that definition), compared as a real.

For all sufficiently large natural n, for every simple graph G whose vertex set is the set {1, 2, ..., n} (Set.Icc 1 n, both endpoints included): if G is triangle-free (CliqueFree 3), then there exist a, b, c in {1,...,n} with a != b, a + b = c (as naturals), and {a, b, c} is an independent set of G (no edge of G joins two of them). (c differs from a and b automatically since a, b >= 1.)

The set of natural numbers n such that Nat.maxPrimeFac(n+1) > Nat.maxPrimeFac(n) (largest prime factor; the values at 0 and 1 are whatever junk values the definition assigns) has natural (asymptotic) density exactly 1/2.

For every infinite set A of natural numbers, there exists a set B of natural numbers with natural density 0 such that every sufficiently large natural n belongs to the sumset A + B = {a + b : a in A, b in B}.

For every finite set S of natural numbers all of whose elements are prime, the set of natural numbers n such that for every p in S the p-adic valuation of n! is even is an infinite set. (S may be empty, in which case the condition is vacuous.)

For every real eps > 0 there exists a real C > 0 such that for every finite set P of points in R^2: the sum, over all u in distanceSet P (the set of distances determined by P, per its definition), of (distanceMultiplicity P u)^2 (the number of pairs at distance u, per its definition, cast to R, squared) is <= C * |P|^(3 + eps), where |P| is cast to R and the exponent is a real power. C depends on eps only.

There exists a real C > 0 such that for every natural n, the diagonal Ramsey number of the n-dimensional hypercube graph Q_n (diagonalGraphRamsey(hypercube n), i.e. R(Q_n, Q_n), cast to R) is <= C * 2^n.

There do NOT exist sets A, B of natural numbers with A infinite and B nonempty such that the sumset A + B is eventually equal, along the cofinite filter, to the set of primes, i.e. A + B and the set of primes differ in only finitely many elements (finite symmetric difference).

For every real C > 0 there exists a natural K >= 3 such that the set of triples (a, b, n) of natural numbers satisfying all of: a > 0, b > 0, n > 0, (a + b as a real) > n + C * log n (natural log, real arithmetic), and for every prime p > K, the p-adic valuation of the denominator of the rational number obtained by casting to Q the NATURAL number n! / (a! * b!) (truncating natural floor division) equals 0 -- is infinite. Note: because the quotient is computed in N and then cast to Q, it is an integer, so its denominator is 1 and the valuation condition holds automatically; thus the statement only requires infinitely many positive triples with a + b > n + C log n.

For every natural n, every coloring color : N -> Fin n, and every natural m, there exists a finite set A of natural numbers with |A| >= m and a color c such that for every nonempty finite subset S of A (a Finset of the subtype A), color(sum of the elements of S) = c and color(product of the elements of S) = c. (A may contain 0 or 1; for n = 0 there is no coloring, so it holds vacuously.)

For all natural x, y with x >= 1 and y >= 1: if for every natural n >= 1 the set of primes p dividing x^n - 1 equals the set of primes p dividing y^n - 1 (natural subtraction, which does not truncate here since x^n, y^n >= 1; note when x = 1, x^n - 1 = 0 and every prime divides 0), then x = y.

There do NOT exist a natural n and a function a : N -> Z such that, with D := {d in N : d divides n and d >= 1}: (1) every integer x satisfies x == a(d) (mod d) for some d in D, and (2) for all d, d' in D with d != d', if some integer x satisfies both x == a(d) (mod d) and x == a(d') (mod d'), then gcd(d, d') = 1. (n = 0 is allowed, in which case D is all positive naturals. Note as written: for n = 1, D = {1}, every integer is congruent to a(1) mod 1, and (2) is vacuous, so such n and a do exist and the negated statement as written is false.)

For every natural k >= 3, for all sufficiently large natural m, for every finite type W and simple graph H on W (decidable adjacency) such that every vertex has positive degree (no isolated vertices) and the edge set of H has exactly m elements (ncard), the graph Ramsey number graphRamsey(C_k, H) (C_k = cycle graph on k vertices) is <= 2m + k/2, where k/2 is truncating natural division (floor(k/2)), and all arithmetic is in N.

There exists a function f : N -> N with f(n) -> infinity as n -> infinity such that for all sufficiently large n there exists a composite natural m with n + f(n) < m < n + minFac(n) (strict inequalities; minFac(n) is the smallest prime factor of n, with junk values minFac 0 = 2, minFac 1 = 1).

For every type V and every simple graph G on V: if the chromatic number of G is infinite (= top in extended naturals), then the function on the set of odd cycle lengths of G, a |-> ((1 / a : N) cast to R), is NOT summable. Important: 1 / a is truncating natural division, equal to 0 for every a >= 2 (and 1 only if a = 1). Since odd cycle lengths in a simple graph are >= 3, every term is 0, the family is summable, and the conclusion is false; as written the statement thus asserts that no simple graph has infinite chromatic number.

For every function c : N -> Bool (2-coloring of the naturals), there exist natural numbers x and d with 0 < x < d such that c(x), c(x+d), c(x+2d) are all equal (to some common value C). Note d must exceed x.

It is NOT the case that: for all naturals r, q and every simple graph H on Fin q, if r > 0, H is bipartite and H is r-degenerate, then the function n |-> extremalNumber n H (cast to R) is Big-O (as n -> infinity) of n |-> n^e (real power), where e is the cast to R of the NATURAL number 2 - 1/r with 1/r truncating natural division and the subtraction truncating. So e = 1 when r = 1 and e = 2 when r >= 2 (not 2 - 1/r as a real). The statement asserts that some r > 0 and bipartite r-degenerate H exist for which ex(n, H) is not O(n^e).

It is NOT the case that: for every real eps with 0 < eps < 1 and every real alpha with 0 < alpha < 1, for all sufficiently large D (eventually in atTop), for all sufficiently large natural n (eventually, with the threshold allowed to depend on D), for every simple graph G on Fin n with number of edges (ncard, as a real) > n^(1+alpha), there exists a subgraph H of G such that, with m := number of vertices of H (ncard), H (as a graph on its vertex subtype) is D-balanced (IsBalanced, per its definition), m > n^(1-alpha), and the number of edges of H > eps * m^(1+alpha) (real powers). Quantifier order: eps, alpha, then eventually D, then eventually n.

For every type V and every simple graph G on V with infinite chromatic number (= top), for every natural N there exists a natural n >= N such that 2^n belongs to the set of cycle lengths of G; i.e. G contains cycles of length 2^n for infinitely many n.

For every natural N there exist a natural n >= N and a simple graph G on Fin n such that G is NOT Ramsey size linear (IsRamseySizeLinear, per its definition), but every subgraph H of G with H strictly less than the top subgraph (i.e. every proper subgraph: missing at least one vertex or at least one edge), viewed as a graph on its vertex subtype, IS Ramsey size linear.
For every natural n >= 2 and every simple graph T on Fin n that is a tree, the diagonal Ramsey number R(T, T) (diagonalGraphRamsey T) is <= 2n - 2 (natural subtraction; no truncation since n >= 2).

For every real K > 0 there exist reals C > 0 and c > 0 such that for every finite set A of integers with |A| >= 2 and |A + A| <= K * |A|^2 (cardinalities cast to R): c * |A|^2 / (log |A|)^C <= |A * A|, where A + A is the sumset, A * A the product set, log the natural logarithm, the power (log|A|)^C a real power, and division real. (Note |A+A| <= |A|^2 always, so for K >= 1 the second hypothesis is automatic.)

It is NOT the case that for every a : N -> N: if (a(n) >= 1 for all natural n, including n = 0) and (the real sequence n |-> 1/a(n) is summable), then there exists a real t >= 1 such that the (unconditional) sum over all n of 1/(a(n) + t) (real division) is irrational. Equivalently: there is a sequence of positive integers with summable reciprocals such that for every real t >= 1, the sum of 1/(a(n)+t) is rational (this sum converges by comparison, so no tsum junk value arises).

For all real alpha and beta, the liminf as n -> infinity (n natural) of the real sequence n * ||n alpha|| * ||n beta|| equals 0, where ||x|| = distToNearestInt x is the distance from x to the nearest integer (n is cast to R).

For every natural k >= 2, the predicate OrdinalRamsey (omega_1)^2 (omega_1)^2 k does NOT hold, where omega_1 is the first uncountable ordinal, (omega_1)^2 is ordinal exponentiation with natural exponent 2, and k is cast to an ordinal; OrdinalRamsey alpha beta gamma is the ordinal partition (arrow) relation as defined in the source, with arguments in this order.

There exists a function o : N -> R with o = O(1) along atTop (o is eventually bounded; Big-O, NOT little-o) such that for all sufficiently large n, (1 - o(n)) * n <= maximalDistinctDistancesFrom n (n cast to R). Note: because only O(1) is required, one may take o to be a large constant making the left side negative, so the statement is essentially trivial whenever maximalDistinctDistancesFrom n is nonnegative.

There exists a function h : N -> N with h(n) -> infinity such that for all naturals n, i, j with 1 <= i < j <= n / 2 (n / 2 is truncating natural division, floor(n/2)), h(n) <= gcd(C(n, i), C(n, j)) (binomial coefficients). For n with no such pair i, j (n < 4) the condition is vacuous.

There do NOT exist a sequence x : N -> Gaussian integers Z[i] and an integer C such that x is injective and, for every n, x(n) is a prime element of Z[i] (Prime in the ring sense) and the norm of x(n+1) - x(n) (the integer a^2 + b^2) is < C. I.e. one cannot walk through infinitely many distinct Gaussian primes with uniformly bounded steps.

For every function f : N -> R satisfying all of: f(n) = 1 or f(n) = -1 for every n >= 1 (f(0) is unconstrained by this clause), f(m n) = f(m) f(n) for all naturals m, n that are coprime (including cases with 0, e.g. m = 0, n = 1), and f(1) = 1, there exists a real L such that (sum over n in Finset.Icc 1 N = {1, ..., N} of f(n)) / N tends to L as N -> infinity, where N is cast to R and the division is real (at N = 0 it is 0/0 = 0).
